title: Act V, Scene II

teacherSummary.text: Scottish thanes (Menteith, Caithness, Angus and Lennox) march to join Malcolm's English power near Birnam Wood. They say Macbeth strongly fortifies Dunsinane; some call him mad, and those he commands 'move only in command, nothing in love.' Angus says Macbeth's title hangs loose about him 'like a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief.' They march to give their blood as medicine to purge their sick country.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.

items.lookFor: Menteith, Caithness, Angus and Lennox.
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?
items.answerGuidance: Menteith, Caithness, Angus and Lennox.

items.text: Retell the most important events of “Act V, Scene II” in order, one sentence for each event.
items.lookFor: Scottish thanes (Menteith, Caithness, Angus and Lennox) march to join Malcolm's English power near Birnam Wood. They say Macbeth strongly fortifies Dunsinane; some call him mad, and those he commands 'move only in command, nothing in love.' Angus says Macbeth's title hangs loose about him 'like a giant's robe upon a dwarfish thief.' They march to give their blood as medicine to purge their sick…
followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.
Who can add a detail that comes just before or after?

items.text: Reread: “Now does he feel His secret murders sticking on his hands; Now minutely revolts upbraid his faith-breach; Those he commands move only in command, Nothing in love: now does he feel his title Hang loose about him, like a…” What does “revolts” mean here, and what is literally happening in this line?

followUps: Where exactly does it say that? Read us the line.

items.answerGuidance: revolts: rebellions.

items.text: What does the clothing image suggest about Macbeth's right to rule?
items.lookFor: He is small inside a role that does not fit; the crown is stolen.

Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: He is small inside a role that does not fit; the crown is stolen.

items.text: What does “Act V, Scene II” suggest about the tyrant's weakening grip? State the inference and the line that supports it.
items.lookFor: Macbeth's own nobles now see him as a usurper too small for the crown. The medical language (purge, sick country) prepares the healing of Scotland.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Macbeth's own nobles now see him as a usurper too small for the crown. The medical language (purge, sick country) prepares the healing of Scotland. Evidence to accept: “now does he feel his title / Hang loose about him, like a giant’s robe / Upon a dwarfish thief” (Act V, Scene II, lines 2081–2083): Clothing imagery. Credit any reading that quotes the text and explains it.

items.text: Find one example of imagery in “Act V, Scene II”. What does it reveal about the tyrant's weakening grip that a plain statement would not?
items.lookFor: Look for sensory details (sight, sound, cold, light) and what mood they create.

Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: Look for sensory details (sight, sound, cold, light) and what mood they create. Evidence to accept: “Those he commands move only in command, / Nothing in love” (Act V, Scene II, lines 2080–2081): His followers obey from fear. Credit any reading that quotes the text and explains it.

items.text: How does the characterization in “Act V, Scene II” shape what we understand about the tyrant's weakening grip?
items.lookFor: Look for what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them.
followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: The rebels see Macbeth as a man too small for the title he stole. Useful evidence: “now does he feel his title / Hang loose about him, like a giant’s robe / Upon a dwarfish thief” (Act V, Scene II, lines 2081–2083): Clothing imagery. On characterization: Scottish thanes desert Macbeth; the rebels march. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

lessonAtAGlance.title: Act V, Scene II
lessonAtAGlance.objective: Students will summarize what happens in Act V, Scene II (the tyrant's weakening grip) in 2 sentences and, in a 3-sentence warm-up response, explain how one quoted line from the scene sets up the scene that follows.
